rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Black prepares to fianchetto their dark-square bishop. From g7 this bishop will exert considerable pressure over the centre and facilitate a queen's side attack. However, 5...g6 weakens Black's kingside pawn structure and encourages White to pursue a king's side attack of their own.
6. Be3 is the main move. This usually leads to the Yugoslav attack, where White castles queen's side and tries to pawn storm on the king's side. Because both players are attacking on opposite wings, there is no time to be lost for either side and subtle manoeuvring will tend to take a back seat to sharp tactics.
6. Be2, the classical variation, is the main alternative, where White prepares to castles short and away Black's powerful bishop. This is a less sharp continuation.
Less common approaches include:
6. f4 is the Levenfish attack. This postpones matters of development to take space and prepare the trappy move e5, an immediate assault on the centre.
6. g3 is the fianchetto variation. This prepares Bg2 and O-O.
6. f3 is a small move order difference, usually transposing into the main line after 6...O-O 7. Be3.
6. Bc4 may transpose into the Yugoslav attack (6...Bg7 7. f3 O-O 8. Be3 Nc6 9. Qd2), or lead to a Sozin attack-style line where White castles short and focuses on piece play rather than a pawn storm.

**History** …

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Black plays 5...a6 and controls the b5 square. This is prophylaxis, removing White's options of Ndb5 or Bb5+, and supports further queenside expansion with ...b5 and ...b4 in the future, which could become dangerous for White should they castle queenside.
Flexibility is a key to this opening: Black chooses to develop their knight to d7 or c6 in some lines; their bishops to b7 or e6 and e7 (if the e-pawn is advanced) or g7 (after ...g6) in different lines.
5...a6 prepares 6...e5, kicking the knight to b3, because the intermezzo 7. Bb5+ is prevented. However, it doesn't make any immediate threats, therefore White has a large variety of ways to continue:

**Develop a bishop**
6. Bg5 is most popular: developing the dark squared bishop actively and threatening to double Black's pawns with an eventual Bxf6. As playing 6...e5 would leave the d5 square too weak, with White having far more control of it than Black, Black usually responds with 6...e6, entering a Scheveningen-type pawn structure.
6. Be3 is the English attack. White plans for a quick attack on the kingside: Qd2 and O-O-O, then a kingside pawn storm with f3, g4, and h4. This usually results in opposite-side castling, with a lot of dynamic play and chances for both sides.
White can also develop the kings bishop:
6. Be2, the Opocensky variation, prepares to castle kingside. This is the calmer, positional move. If 6...e5, White exploits pressure on the weak d5 square. …

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
5... e6, building a so-called "small center", is the signature move of the Scheveningen Variation of the Sicilian Defence. 5... e6 strengthens Black's control of the important d5 square and opens e7 for the development of his dark-squared bishop. If Black is able to safely play ... d5 later on, he will have a good position.
In contrast to the Najdorf Variation, 5... a6, the Scheveningen commits Black earlier to a certain pawn structure in the center and delays queenside operations, but does more to promote Black's early development and castling. Both systems are considered very solid choices for Black, however 5... a6 has been played by even the best Scheveningen specialists (including Garry Kasparov) to avoid the dangerous Keres Attack, 5... e6 6. g4!  (Although by no means winning for White, statistics sharply favour the white pieces.)

rn1qkbnr/p1ppp2p/1p4P1/7Q/3P4/3B4/PPP2Pb.text:
Taking black's g-pawn, and threatening black's h-pawn. Black can now play:

6...Nf6, a grave error - attempting to scare off white's queen, but in reality dooming black to mate in 2.
6...Bg7, a much better move, but after 7. Qf5! Nf6 8. Bh6 Bxh6 9. gxh7 e6! (weaker are 9...Bxh1 10. Qg6+ Kf8 11. Qxh6+ Kf7 12. Nh3, when White has a winning attack, and 9...Kf8 10. Qg6 Bc1 11. Qxg2 Bxb2 12.Ne2 and 13.Rg1 will prove lethal) 10. Qg6+ Ke7 11. Qxg2 and White is two pawns up and Black's king is exposed, but Black is not immediately losing and has avoided the worst, and the pawn on h7 will fall.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/1n1p4/8/2PP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text: Black would very much like to put pressure on the d-pawn with ...Nc6 and ...Bg7. Playing 6...Nc6 now however runs into d4-d5, maybe even on the next move, and the knight will find itself kicked around the board. So Black is in most games patient, and plays 6...g6 to prepare 7...Bg7.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1n6/4P3/2PP4/8/PP4PP/R.text:
The white center is now very strong. Black has two main options to counter it.

6...Nc6 attacks the d4 pawn. This pawn cannot be pushed as the e pawn would be left en prise.
6...c5 is far riskier. After 7. d5, Black can be strangled. This game is going to be very tactical.
6...Bf5 is also possible & keeps the option of ...c5 before ...Nc6, but it tends to transpose into 6...Nc6.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2P5/4PP2/2N2N2/PP.text: White chooses the simplest option, taking the pawn. Black's next move wins back a pawn and achieves a better pawn structure. The other option for White would be to ignore Black's threats and lose the pawn, in addition to getting an inferior position.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p1b1/3pP3/3P2P1/2N5/P.text: White threatens Nf4 and h4, so Black must react. Black usually counters in the centre with 6... c5.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3pP3/3P4/3QB3/PPP2.text: From here, after say 6...Nd7, white could look to play, the knights to f3 and d2, with a solid centre, and a solid pawn structure. Castling, followed by g4 and f5 leads to an interesting kingside attack, while the queenside is fairly safe.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP.text: With this move, White immediately threatens the d5 pawn. Here, Black can simply capture the c pawn with 6...dxc4, or defend the d pawn with 6...e6 or even the strange-looking but perfectly sound 6...Be6, when Black usually fianchettos the dark-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.text: 6. Nf3 is the main line for white, and black has a number of alternatives here. The more solid 6... e6, fianchettoing the bishop with 6... g6, or the main line, 6... Bg4, which leads to somewhat crazy positions that black can safely navigate if they know what they're doing.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pNp1/2p2n1p/8/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White grabs the f7 pawn with 6. Nxf7?, entering the dubious but incredibly scary Alien Gambit, popularized by YouTuber Witty Alien! This gambit is losing for White and can be punished with careful play; as such, it is mostly used in Bullet and Blitz.
The purpose of this move is to ruin Black's kingside structure by creating several light-squared holes in Black's kingside; force the Black king to recapture, giving up castling rights; and take Black out of their comfort zone, since most Caro-Kann players are mostly used to slow, positional grinds rather than tactical skirmishes. The Alien Gambit is an attack on Black's weak light squares on the kingside. When the knight grabs the f7 pawn, Black has several light-squared holes on e6 and g6 which can quickly be pounced on by White's pieces, often leading to checkmate for White on these very squares.
Black has two approaches to send the aliens back to their desolate sector of the cosmos: one is to attack White's weak dark squares with c5, Nc6, and so on; another is to defend the light squares with Be6, develop the knight with Nbd7, and counterattack on the light squares. Both of these approaches can even be combined seamlessly, leading to the aliens' demise.
Black must respect White's attack on the light squares. After Nxf7? Kxf7 Nf3 Bg4?? (which is the most common response), White can play Ne5! and win the knight back with a monstrous attack on the light squares to follow.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP.text: Black needs to defend the bishop, and h6 is almost universal, although the probably inferior h5 and Nd7 have been attempted.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p3b1/8/3P4/5NN1/PPP2PP.text: 6... Nd7 is by far the most popular response, to prevent a possible Ne5

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2np4/8/2B1P3/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White's bishop pressures Black's vulnerable f7 pawn. The strength of the bishop's pressure can be seen in a number of traps Black can fall into with imprecise play. Black can blunt its attack by pushing the pawn ...e6, though the question is, now or later?
6...e6 is the most straight forward and main move. This reaches a Scheveningen-style structure, otherwise reached after the line 5...e6 6. Bc4 d6. This only requires a small amount of patience: Black is preparing to play ...e5 and to allow the bishop back into the game. The line continues 7. O-O Nf6 8. Qe2 Be7 9. Rd1 e5 10. Be3 O-O 11. Rac1.
Playing ...e5 in two moves (6...e6 then 9...e5) looks like a waste of tempo, but it is necessary for Black to manage the pressure on f7. 6...e5? allows 7. Ng5! for an attack on f7. 7...Nh6 8. Qf3 f6 is forced, but this allows 9. Ne6! Bxe6 10. Bxe6 ±. Black may think they have Nd4 with tempo and Nc2+, however Black can quickly become undone. 10...Nd4 11. Qh3 and White threatens Bxh6!! (the bishop cannot be recaptured because of Qh5+ and Qf7#!). 11...Nc2+ 12. Kf1 does nothing about the threat of Bxh6. 11. Nxe6? 12. Qxe6 Qe7 13. Qc4 and White threatens Nd4, Bxh6, and Black's position is tied up in knots.
But by first playing ...e6, the bishop's pressure on f7 is nullified while Black plays ...Be7, ...Nf6 and ...O-O. Then, with their rook guarding f7, it is safe enough for Black to push ...e5. In this way, ...e6 is necessary preparation for ...e5. …

r1bqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2n2n2/1N2p3/4P3/2N5/PP.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5
The White knight's threat of check on d6 is a bit awkward: ...Ke7 would be unpleasant so Black would have to surrender his bishop with ...Bxd6, only to have a queen arrive on d6 and single-handedly cramp the whole Black position. She would need to go, too: ...Qe7 Qxe7 Kxe7/Nxe7, and suddenly Black's dodgy d-pawn and slow development are significant factors in the much simplified position. Far better to keep the knight out of d6 for now and then vanquish it to a3 in a move's time with 6...d6.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/8/2PNP3/4B3/PP3P.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3

6...Nf6:

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2npp3/1N6/2P1P3/8/PP3PPP.text:
White sets up the Maroczy bind structure to control d5. Between their c and e pawns, and having induced Black to play d6 and restrict their own dark square bishop, they hope to keep Black's position cramped, hampering their development, and that this will make up for the loss of tempo White incurred in moving their knight multiple times in the opening.
If 6...a6 straight away, Black kicks White's knight and they are forced to move it again: usually to c3.
Black usually plays 6...Nf6 first, threatening Nxe4 with the idea of inducing 7. N1c3, followed by 7...a6 to kick the knight to 8. Na3 where it is on the rim and therefore grim, but from where it overprotect the c4 pawn and doesn't obstruct the White queen's support of d5.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np1n2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
6.Bc4 begins the Sozin attack on the classical Sicilian. Black may choose to reply with e6, which is a position easily reached through transposition from the Scheveningen variation as well (6.Bc4,Nc3). However, from the Scheveningen variation white tends to pick other attacks which are more suited to the position, such as the English Attack or the Keres Attack. The Sozin attack is often considered less common and less ambitious than the Richter-Rauzer Attack.
Black could also choose to reply with g6 transposing to a form of the Dragon variation, but this leads to the "Magnus Smith trap," with a lot of trouble for black (see a YouTube analysis here).
If black does play e6, both players typically develop bishops with white playing Be3 and black responding with Be7. In this position if white castles king side it is called the Fisher-Sozin attack. If white instead moves Qe2 and eventually castles queenside it is called the Velimirovic variation.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2np1n2/6B1/3NP3/2N5/PPP.text:
Traditionally, in the Classical Sicilian, Black aims for ...e5 or ...g6. The Richter-Rauser (also spelt Richter-Rauzer) is a way for white to combat both of these ideas. It does not completely stop either of the ideas, but it does make them less desirable. ...g6 would weaken the defense of the Black knight on f6.
6...e5 in this position would be considered winning for White and detrimental to the Black position, as after White captures the knight with 7. Bxf6, Black has to choose between capturing back with the g-pawn, or with the Queen:
Option 1: Taking back with 7...gxf6 is the better of the two options according to engine analysis, although it comes with White gaining an outpost for its knight after 8. Nf5. Black could attempt to dislodge the knight with 9...d5, but this can be met with 10. Qxd5. Exchanging Queens immediately is not good for Black, as after 10...Qxd5 11. Nxd5, White is threatening to fork the Black King and Rook with Nc7+. Black is forced to exchange its Light-Squared Bishop with 11...Bxf5 12. exf5. Black then castles with 12...O-O-O, and White wins a pawn.
Option 2: Taking back on f6 with the Black Queen (7...Qxf6) is the worst of the two options and gives White double the advantage. White moves his knight with 8. Ndb5 threaten Nc7+, forking the King and Rook. Defending with the Queen isn't feasible, as White can simply place his other knight on d5 with a nice outpost, and c7 is weak again. …

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP1B.text: This variation is a variation of the Sicilian tradition of the dragon. White wants to make a great defence in kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
6. Bc4 is an older sideline, very similar to the Fischer-Sozin attack in the Najdorf and the Scheveningen. White seeks to better control d5 and exert pressure on the black king, especially the f7 square. It also keeps options open for white, on whether to transpose into the mainline Yugoslav or play a more quiet, maneuvering game. Black almost always proceeds with Bg7, looking to castle fast.
If white doesn't transpose into the Yugoslav Attack, this variation is considered not sharp enough for black, which is why it has fallen out of favour. Black gets a fantastic middlegame with a very nice pawn structure and easy plans, whereas white has no immediate pressure and doesn't use the extra tempo effectively.
It is worth noting that formally this variation doesn't have a name or separate code in the ECO. Informally, some call it the Sozin or the Italian Attack.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NPP2/2N5/PPP3.text:
This move has a few ideas connoted to it. The primary idea is to push e5, since this pawn idea gains central influence and is now prepared by f4. White can also look to put the knight back onto f3 and play the position like a Grand Prix attack, with future ideas of swinging the white queen onto the kingside through the e1-h4 diagonal. Against some sidelines, white can also consider castling long!

**The point - 6...Bg7?! 7. e5!**
The natural looking 6...Bg7 is actually theoretically inaccurate. This runs into White's primary idea of the Levenfish, to push e5. White does this immediately with 7. e5 and then can claim a slight, nagging edge in the upcoming variations because of the advanced e-pawn.
White should seek active play with Bb5+ and Qe2 to support the pawn before deciding which way to castle, both leading to viable positions

**Main Line - 6...Nc6**
The best move since it immediately covers the threat of e5. This idea effectively killed the Levenfish variation pre-2000. Black develops the queenside knight. Here, White has traditionally gone for the line 7. Nxc6!? bxc6 8. e5 which is somewhat favourable for black upon 8...Nd7! 9. exd6 exd6 leading to an interesting pawn structure. A sounder alternative several high profile games have included is the idea of 7. Nf3!? swinging the knight back to the kingside and looking to play a slower game on the kingside. …

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
White develops their bishop. This prepares to castle queenside and usually leads to the Yugoslav attack.
6...Bg7 is the most logical and main line continuation, developing the bishop as prepared by ...g6 and preparing to castle.
6...Nc6 is an alternative. This is really a waiting move where Black delays committing their bishop. 7. f3 h5 is the Hungarian variation, and Black has the idea of meeting 8. Qd2 with 8...Nxd4 9. Bxd4 Bh6! 10. Be3 Bxe3 11. Qxe3, trading off the minor pieces and so easing the discomfort of being down on space.
If Black is tempted to play 6...Ng4??, hoping to chop off White's dark-squared Bishop and leave their bishop unopposed, they should be warned that this a beginner's mistake which loses horribly to 7. Bb5+.

7...Nd7 8. Qxg4 wins the knight.
7...Bd7 8. Qxg4 also wins the knight, since the Bishop on d7 is pinned.
7...Nc6 8. Nxc6 bxc6 9. Bxc6+, forking the king and rook and winning the exchange and a pawn.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
6. Be3 is the English attack. White has an idea to castle long and storm Black's kingside with their pawns.
6...e5 is the main line. This drives off White's knight to b3, but weakens d5 which White will try to use as an outpost.
6...Ng4 is the Anti-English. Black tries to avert White's plans of a kingside attack by trading off White's important dark square bishop. Whereas in the Yugoslav attack against the Dragon Sicilian, 6. Be3 Ng4?? is a mistake on account of 7. Bb5+! Nc6 8. Nxc6 bxc6 9. Bxc6+ Bd7 10. Bxa8, the difference in the Najdorf is that Black has played ...a6, so White does not have the resource Bb5+, therefore ...Ng4 is safe.
6...e6 builds a "small centre" and transposes into a Scheveningen Scillian. This is move order ju-jitsu to play the Scheveningen without facing the Keres attack, 5...e6 6. g4!. In that line, Black cannot play 6...e5 on account of the Bb5+ resource. However, in the move order 5...a6 6. Be3 e6, Black's a6 pawn prevents Bb5+, so 7. g4!? can be met with ...e5!, a discovered attack on g4 and threatening ...exd4 with a fork.

**History**
6. Be3 is the most popular way for White to combat the Najdorf. It has been played since the 1950s, but 6. Bg5 was more typical until the 1980s, when 6. Be3 was popularised by English grandmasters like Tony Miles, John Nunn and Nigel Short.
The approach--long castle and pawn storm--had been the standard approach against the Dragon Sicilian, the Yugoslav attack, since at least the 1930s.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP2P.text:
With 6. Be3, white begins a standard English attack setup. White will play f3, g4, Qd2 and O-O-O in some order, setting up a kingside pawn storm targeted towards black's king. In response, black will play a6 and b5 and set up a pawn attack on the queenside against white's king.
Note that the standard 6...a6 from black transposes into a hybrid Najdorf/Scheveningen, and allows white to begin the Perenyi Attack with 7.g4 if desired.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/8/3NP1P1/2N5/PPP2P.text:
White's 6. g4 begins the Keres Attack, a sharp and important line in the Scheveningen Variation.
Black's previous move, 5...e6, boxes in his light squared bishop and relinquishes control over the g4 square. Now, White advances his g pawn with the idea of following with 7. g5, pushing black's f knight back and winning more space on the kingside. Note that against the Sicilian, White often opens up a kingside pawn storm, such as in the English Attack, and 6. g4 furthers that goal well.
Black's most common response, therefore, is 6...h6, preventing the g pawn from advancing. Other responses, such as 6...Nc6, do not discourage the g pawn push, and are therefore usually followed by 7. g5 Nd7. Now black's kingside knight has been pushed back into a much more passive position and white's pawns are dangerously close to black's kingside, if black chooses to castle there. After 6...h6 Black should certainly not proceed to castle kingside quickly against this line.
Attempting to counterattack with 6...e5 is easily met by 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nb3. White has traded off light squared bishops, and is preparing to set up the standard English Attack. Note that this is one reason that many Scheveningen players use a Najdorf move order first and transpose to the Scheveningen. In this case, the presence of the a6 pawn discourages Bb5+, and lines here in which white plays g4 are referred to as the Perenyi Attack rather than the Keres Attack.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP1B.text:
Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Be2
6. Be2 is not played as often in response to black pushing 5. ...a6 as is 6. Bg5 or 6. Be3, but it is a solid move. White's bishop at e2 can keep an eye on g4 while allowing for a king side castle.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3ppn2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
White enters the Sozin Attack, a direct and aggressive system named after Russian master Veniamin Sozin. By placing the bishop on c4, White eyes the vulnerable f7 square and sets the stage for a fast kingside assault. This move fits perfectly against the Scheveningen setup, where Black’s e6 pawn can make the light squares around the king more tender.
Typical ideas for White include Qe2, Bb3, 0–0, and f4–f5, often leading to sharp play. In response, Black must tread carefully—failing to play ...Be7 and ...0–0 promptly can invite devastating attacks. The Sozin is a favorite of players seeking initiative and imbalances, and was famously wielded by Bobby Fischer with great success.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
6. Bc4
White develops her light-squared bishop to c4, entering the Fischer-Sozin attack. Pioneered by Fischer who extensively developed the theory of it, taking inspiration from Sozin's 6. Bc4 againt the Classical Sicilian, this move was at one point White's main weapon of choice against the Najdorf. However, it then fell out of favor as ways for Black to effectively equalise against it have been found, while the English Attack's true potential to pose problems for black was discovered. Recently, it has made a resurgence with modern lines that have strong practical value.
While the bishop may be a target on c4, it eyes the f7 square against Black's king. Naturally, Black almost always responds with ...e7-e6, closing the bishop's diagonal towards the f7 square. Then, White has a few ways to develop, though she usually plays the improving move Bb3, moving the bishop to a safer square and in anticipation of ...b7-b5:
-The classical way to play this variation is to castle kingside, then launch the f-pawn forward to pressure Black's light squares and start a same-side kingside attack. While this line might be playable, it has been shown that black could equalise without facing major problems from white. The modern improvement to this variant is to first play Qf3-Qg3, making the queen an active contributor in the attack.
-Modern systems planning to castle queenside are promising. …

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/8/3NP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
The Freak Attack is a very recent and upcoming response to the Najdorf. White's idea is to prepare a quick g2-g4, in style of the Keres Attack, combined with h4 and f4 causing problems to black's kingside. It also allows the bishop to develop to h3 in the future. Even though Rg1 looks absurd at first glance, it is a totally sound option according to the strongest engines. It is also a great surprise weapon - Theory is still developing on it and engine lines are still not sure how to proceed.
Of course, like every move, it is not the best choice either. White has forfeited kingside castling, so black can concentrate on the center and the queenside instead. White also leaves a massive hole on f3 -- While covered for now by the knight and the queen, black can later make use of the backward f2 pawn. And finally, black can prevent white's apparent plan with an immediate h5, which also has a massive winrate so far.
The antidote to the entire variation is considered to be ...e5 Nb3 Be6 g4 d5!. Black strikes back in the center and a series of trades occur leaving both sides with a minimal amount of pieces to proceed into the game, and white's kingside assault plan is halted before it even starts.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/6B1/3NP3/2N5/PPP.text:

6...Nbd7 is also playable.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP4/8/PP4PP/.text: The so-called Alekhine Knights come out to attack White's center, with d4 under attack. White must now defend the pawn. The main line is 7.Be3. 7.Nf3 is strongly met by 7...Bg4 with strong pressure on the center.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/q1P5/4PP2/2N2N2/P.text:
With this move Black regains the pawn. Here are some sample variations:

7.cxd6 Nxe4 8.Bd2 (8.dxe7 Nxc3) Nxd6, with a better position for Black.
7.Bd3 Qxc5, when white is slighty better, because white can play 8.Qe2 with the idea of 9.Be3 and white also have more space.

**In other positions**
This is not the only position in which this tactic will appear. There are many other variations which involve this equalization trick for Black. For example, consider the moves 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Bg7 5.h4 c5! After White's forced 6.dxc5 (6.Nf3 Qa5!) Qa5! 7.Bd3 Qxc5, again with a much better pawn structure. Black can get this dominant, healthy pawn structure in many Pirc variations. Certainly the Black pawns are better than the White pawns. Black has strong pressure on White's e-pawn. Meanwhile, White has weakened his kingside with his now-useless move 5.h4. The point of this move was to play 6.h5, creating a weakness in the Black kingside, but now the g3 and g4 squares are weakened, and it is White's position that gets the weakness.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/2PP2b1/2N2N2/P.text: White has their eye on the weak points in black's position, b7 and d5, and most commonly takes on d5 with the pawn here. However, 7. Be3, 7. Bg5, and 7. Be2 are also perfectly playable.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/6B1/2pP4/2N5/PP3P.text: 6... dxc5 results in the classic isolated queen's pawn position. White usually recaptures the pawn, offering up the d pawn for a healthy lead in development, but can also push to d5, or develop the knight to f3.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppp/2p3b1/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
While Nd7 seems inferior because of the weak bishop, this was never tested in the only instance this move was played at master level, between Rustam Kasimdzhanov and Mikhael Mchedlishvili in the European Clubs Cup (Men) in 2003. (That game quickly transposed back to a main line, continuing: 6...Nd7 7. Nf3 h6 8. h5 Bh7 9. Bd3 Bxd3 10. Qxd3 e6 11. Bf4 Ngf6 12. O-O-O Be7 13. Kb1 O-O 14. Ne4 Qa5 15. g4 Nxg4 16. Ne5 Ndxe5 17. dxe5 Rad8 18. Qh3 Qb4 19. Rdg1 Qxe4 20. Rxg4 Qh7 21. Rhg1 Kh8 22. Qg3 Rg8 23. Be3 a6 24. a3 Rd7 25. Qg2 Rd5 26. Qg3 Rd7 27. Qg2 Rd5 28. Qg3 1/2-1/2.)
It may appear at first that White can trap the bishop, but this is not the case after 7. h5 Bf5 8. Nxf5 Qa5+! +=. However, White can do this anyway and get the bishop pair and light-square control.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3b1/7p/3P3P/6N1/PPP2P.text: Instead of the more traditional ...h6, here black opts to block the white pawn from advancing altogether. This is a rare move at the professional level, although not an inherently bad one (although castling kingside becomes more dangerous compared to ...h6 lines). White has a large variety of moves to play; 7. Nf3 develops a piece while 7. Nh3!?, aiming for an eventual Nf4, has also been attempted.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3bp/8/3P3P/6N1/PPP2PP.text: 7. Nf3 is almost always played, with white aiming to place the knight on e5. White's other options have rarely been seen in master play.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppp/2p3b1/8/3P4/5NN1/PPP2PP.text: White again has a large list of options, some of which transpose to other lines. h4 will probably transpose to the most popular line (h4 is more commonly played on move 6).

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np1n2/1N2p3/4P3/2N5/PPP.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6
A little fact that is often forgotten by Sveshnikov players: the d5 square is genuinely weak and likely to remain so. Black's activity doesn't come easy but as compensation for taking on that weakness - an important distinction. White therefore has a logical mini-plan: occupy d5, preferably with a knight, preferably one that can't be instantly captured.
The immediate Nd5 has its followers, as the e-pawn is clearly immune from capture due to Nbc7+. This line was chosen four times by Fabiano Caruana in the World Chess Championship 2018 match against Magnus Carlsen. After Black plays 7...Nxd5, the nice outpost vanishes after 8.exd5 (8.Qxd5 a6 9. Nc3 Be6 is miserable - capturing on d5 with the queen is usually a sign that something's gone wrong). One plan for black is to play 8...Nb8 with ...Nd7 and ...f5 to follow. In their match, Carlsen also tried 8...Ne7 9.c4 Ng6.
White more often pins down the f6 knight with Bg5 - it's important to see this move as a means of increasing control of d5, rather than just pinning a knight out of boredom.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP.text:
Black develops their knight to its natural square where it controls the centre, and prepares to castle.
7. f3?! is the most common move in amateur games, but it is inaccurate. White thinks to play in the manner of the Yugoslav attack, where f3 is necessary to defend e4 and control g4, preventing ...Ng4 and freeing the queen to move to d2. However, in this line, after 7...O-O 8. Qd2, Black has 8...d5!. Compared to the regular dragon, Black saved a tempo by skipping ...d6 and so played ...d5 one turn earlier, before White has had the chance to long castle. White doesn't have the time to deliver their crushing kingside attack and Black has achieved equality.
The modern line is 7. Bc4. By increasing control of d5, White takes the sting out of ...d5 so that they can continue the plan of opposite side castling. It is still possible for White to err in move order here: 7...O-O 8. f3?! is a common inaccuracy on account of 8...Qb6, a double attack on b2 and d4 which threatens the sacrifice ...Nxe4. 8. Be3 must be included to protect b2.
7. Be2, intending 7...O-O 8. O-O, is an alternative. The line continues 8...d5 9. exd5 Nxd5 10. Nxd5 Qxd5 11. Bf3.
7. Nxc6 is another minor side line. This differs from the exchange variation (5. Nxc6) in that White intends 7...bxc6 8. e5, attacking Black's other knight.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/2BNP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Black continues with the regular plan of fianchettoing the dark squared bishop. Both sides will continue by castling and entering the middlegame. White will try to play actively in the center and try to eliminate the bishop on g7, whereas black will use that bishop to pressure the center and the queenside.
Alternatively, black can try to transpose into the Yugoslav attack with f3, Qd2, O-O-O and launching a pawn storm at black's king. However, black can prevent this since Bc4 is premature in this position and should be played later on.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP2.text:
7. f3 is the main move. This controls the g4-square and so denies Black ...Ng4, therefore allows White to play Qd2 next and castle long (the Bb5+ idea, which refuted 6...Ng4??, is less powerful now that Black's king can access f8). The pawn on f3 also supports the e4 pawn, liberating the knight from that duty, and can support a king-side pawn storm (g4, h4, g5, h5).
7. Be2 transposes to the classical variation. This allows White to castle short instead, 7...O-O 8. O-O Nc6, with the idea of playing f4 and perhaps e5 (9. Nb3 Be6 10. f4 Qc8 is the Tartakower line), or attacking down the centre with Qd2 and Rad1 (9. Qd2 Bd7 10. Rad1, the battery variation). This sideline is much quieter but has been employed by many players.
7. Qd2!? immediately allows 7...Ng4 8. Bg5 h6 9. Bh4 Nc6, and it is more awkward for White to launch an attack.
7. Bc4 almost always transposes into the old main line following 7...O-O 8. f3 Nc6 9. Qd2.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/8/3NP1n1/2N1B3/PP.text:
Black attacks White's bishop, but falls into a common amateur trap.
White's queen attack's Black's knight, but it is currently guarded by their light square bishop. 7. Bb5+ cuts off that protection.
If Black blocks the check with 7...Nd7, their bishop no longer guards g4. If 7...Bd7, the bishop becomes pinned and so also does not guard g4.
If 7...Nc6, White can trade knights, 8. Nxc6 (attacking the queen) bxc6, and 9. Bxc6+ forks the king and rook.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/8/3NP3/2N1B3/PPP2.text:
This move order is a common transpositional tool for Scheveningen players to avoid the Keres Attack, which is reached from 6.g4 from a standard Scheveningen position. While it initially follows the Najdorf move order, the e6 push is more characteristic of the Scheveningen than the Najdorf, where black often plays a direct e7-e5 push.
Note that here, white can choose to follow up with 7. g4, but this line is referred to as the Perenyi Attack rather than the Keres Attack. This is because now that a6 controls the b5 square, black can play 7...e5 without fear of 8.Bb5+. Normally, in the Keres Attack, that would result in a trade of light squared bishops. But in this case, black now has two attackers on the exposed g4 pawn, where there is only one defender, the white queen. Further, 7...e5 threatens the d4 knight, so simply moving 8.h3 to protect the g pawn drops the knight. White's move, therefore, in the mainline Perenyi Attack, is 8.Nf5, cutting off the bishop's assault on g4 while moving the knight to temporary safety.
White can also play the move 7.f3, following the normal English attack plan of castling queenside. The main line is 7...b5 8. Qd2 Nbd7 9.0-0-0 Bb7 10.a3. This is a very sharp line where White wants to attack on the kingside and keep his control of the center, and Black wants to attack on the queenside and break White's central control. The plans usually revolve around White pushing g4 favorably and Black pushing d5 favorably. …

rnbqkb1r/pp3pp1/3ppn1p/8/3NP1P1/2N5/PPP2.text:
White's 6. g4 begins the Keres Attack, a sharp and important line in the Scheveningen Variation. Black's 6...h6 is the standard continuation, preventing an advance to g5 which would force the f6 knight to retreat.
Now White has a number of options. These include advancing anyway with g5 and exchanging pawns or continuing the pawn storm with h4, h3 or f3.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2p1n2/4p3/3NP3/2N1B3/PP.text:
6...e5 is the most popular and most unbalancing response to the English attack. The pawn drives off the White's well-placed knight from d4 to a more passive square. Although this creates an outpost on d5, Black is saying, basically, that it is irrelevant to the play on the wings, while White is saying that Black will be lost if d5 is occupied.
White must save their knight, usually to 7. Nb3, and Black's main move is 7...Be6, increasing their control of d5. White's plans include playing f3, Qd2, long castling, and storm on the kingside with pawns.
Less popular is 7. Nf3, where the threat of Ng5 discourages 7...Be6. The knight prevents f3 and puts the pawn-storm idea on the back-burner. White concentrates on fighting for control of the d5 square instead.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p4/8/3NP1n1/2N1B3/PPP.text:
Whereas in the dragon sicilian this move is a blunder, here it is totally safe to play it. The idea is simple: Prevent white from getting the English Attack setup by trading the valuable bishop on e3. There are two main variations:

7. Bc1 is sometimes used to quickly draw the game by repetition, since black wants the bishop and white doesn't give that bishop, repeating moves instead. It is however playable just fine, for example, black can continue with Nf6 Bg5 e6, transposing into another line.
7. Bg5 is the alternative: White wants to place the bishop on g3 and continue the setup normally.
7. Qd2?! allows black to get the bishop pair and gain an extra tempo. White doesn't score as well but it can be a surprise weapon at times.

**Theory**
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Be3 Ng4

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p2p1n2/6B1/3NP3/2N5/PP.text:
Moves: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 Nbd7
This knight move is a natural one in the Najdorf, and it also stops Bxf6, doubling the Black pawns. Although not as popular as the move 6...e6, it is a solid, respectable alternative to the main line. Both sides will usually castle queenside. Black, using his knights and light-squared bishop, will attempt to pressure e4. White, on the other hand, will try to get play on the a2-g8 diagonal and the central files.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/6B1/3NP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6
White's offensive should go on with 7. f4, the most popular move. Queen's moves are also possible as well as 7. Be2 but are considered less ambitious.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/1nn5/4P3/2PP4/4B3/PP4P.text: With this move, White defends the d4-pawn with the bishop while not allowing the ...Bg4 pin. Black now almost always plays 7...Bf5, since that is the only logical square for the bishop. Then White plays 8.Nc3 and then Black plays 8...e6, and now White plays 9.Nf3 when Black has a choice between several moves.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/4p1b1/2ppP3/3P2PP/2N5/PP.text: Black must save the bishop, and their most active response is 7... h5. At first 7... h6 looks preferable, as after 8. Nf4 it allows the bishop to retreat and the pawn to be safe, but Black can safely give up the h pawn in exchange for counterplay on the queenside.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QPB4/P.text: Qc8 is most common, though Qd7 allows the option of queenside castling, as well as Rc8.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3P4/3P2b1/2N2N2/PP.text: Following 7. cxd5, there is no good alternative beyond black recapturing with the knight.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3bp/7P/3P4/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
This move attacking the bishop again is inferior due to it wasting two tempi on moving the h-pawn.

**Nimzowitsch Variation: 7...Bh7 8. Rh4!?**
The Nimzowitsch Variation is a rare line of the Caro-Kann that develops the rook early but creates some complications for black.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p3bp/8/3P3P/5NN1/PPP2P.text: The white knight on e5 is usually seen as too powerful, and black normally chooses Nd7 to prevent this.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2np1n2/1N2p1B1/4P3/2N5/P.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 7. Bg5
Pinning the knight on f6 is whites main continuation in this line. This increases the pressure on d5 by taking one of the defenders out and also protects the e4 pawn, which is very important if the knight on c3 gets driven away by blacks b-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/2BNP3/2N1B3/PP.text:
This is the main line. White develops their bishop and increases control of d5 before playing f3. This prevents Black's rejoinder 8...d5, that otherwise equalises against the move order 7. f3 O-O 8. Qd2.
After 7...O-O, the main move, White must first move their bishop again, 8. Bb3, before continuing with f3 (controlling g4), Qd2, and O-O-O. Otherwise, 8. f3?! is answered with 8...Qb6!, 8. Qd2? with 8...Ng4!, exposing an attack on d4 while attacking White's dark square bishop.
7...Qa5!? is a sideline. This compels White to give up on the idea of long castling.

The immediate threat is that 7...Qa5 pins the knight, so 8. Qd2? hangs the e-pawn. 8...Nxe4 9. Nxc6 Qxc3 10. Qxc3 Bxc3+ 11. bxc3 dxc6 ∓.
8. f3 Qb4 threatens to take the bishop. 9. Bb3 Nxe4! and it turns out the f-pawn wasn't enough to protect the e-pawn, as Black has now unleashed three attacks on d4. 10. fxe4? Bxd4 11. Bxd4 Qxd4 12. Qf3 ∓.
8. Nb3 attacks the queen, but can also be met with 8...Qb4 threatening to take the bishop. The line may continue e.g. 9. Nd2 Qxb2 10. Nb5 Qe5 ∓.
Therefore White's best play is 8. O-O, unpinning the knight and defending the e-pawn. If Black continues with 8...Qb4?! anyway, then 9. Qe2 defends the bishop and the b-pawn is poisonous. (9...Qxb2 10. Ncb5 Nxe4 11. Rab1 Nc3 12. Rxb2 Nxe2+ 13. Bxe2 +-.)
Alternatively 7...d6 transposes into the regular dragon variation.

**History** …

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/2PNP3/2N1B3/PP.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3

7...Ng4: Breyer Variation

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2nppn2/1N6/2P1P3/2N5/PP3.text:
7. N1c3 defends White's e4 pawn while developing their knight.
Black usually continues 7...a6, compelling White to retreat to the passive a6 square. However, at least from there White will overprotect the c4 pawn and keep d5 in sight of their queen.
Black can delay a6 until after they have castled: 7...Be7 8. Be2 9. O-O O-O 10. a6.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/4P3/3N1P2/2N5/PPP.text: White still isn't winning a tempo, but "trading pawns" is met with that fate!

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PPP.text:
White's f-pawn defends e4, freeing the c3-knight from the duty, and controls the g4-square. This prevents ...Ng4, which Black was threatening to play and gain time on White's bishop. The pawn on f3 is critical for supporting a king's side attack with g4, h4, and h5 in the future, where White aims to take advantage of the "hook" in the Black king's side, the g6 pawn.
7...O-O is the main move, which gets the king to safety, and aims to setup a sharp and exciting game involving opposite-sides castling.
7...Nc6 is the Belezky line. Usually this is just a small move order difference, and transposes to the main line after 8. Qd2 O-O. However, seeing that White is already preparing to storm the king's side, Black's idea may be to avoid castling completely.
7...a6!? is an alternative. The move ...a6 on turn five is the start of the Najdorf variation, so this line that mixes the Najdorf with the dragon is given the twee name dragondorf. That's where the similarities end, though: the usual way of combatting the English attack (the Yugoslav's cousin in the Najdorf) involves ...e5 and ...Be6, where ...a6 serves to prevent Nb5 or Bb5+, but a pawn on e5 is hardly desirable in the Dragon with Black's bishop on g7. Instead the idea of ...a6 in the dragondorf is usually to support ...b5, and Black plays with a queen's side fianchetto and avoids castling.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2p1n2/4p3/4P3/1NN1B3/PP.text:
White saves their knight. Black now needs to develop their pieces.
They usually begin 7...Be6, which increases their control of the d5 square, a potential outpost for White, while eyeing White's queenside (where Black anticipates White may castle). White continues 8. f3, preventing ...Ng4 and preparing to attack on the kingside with a brute-force pawn storm and long castling. This might take the form 8...Be7 9. Qd2 O-O 10. O-O-O Nbd7 11. g4. If Black obstructs those plans, as with 8...h5 to prevent g4, White switches tack to prioritise the skirmish for d5 and fight in the centre instead.
7...Be7 is another move-order, and is good as long as Black intends to follow up with ...Be6.
The knight is developed later, after the queen's bishop is developed and ...Nbd7 won't block it in. (...Nc6 is contraindicated: as Black may want use of the half-open c-file and the knight may need to route to b6 to control d5 and c4).

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/8/3NP1P1/2N1B3/PP.text:
The Perenyi Attack is similar in idea to its cousin the Keres Attack of the standard Scheveningen Variation. White mounts an aggressive pawn storm on the kingside, castling long and supporting with Be3 and Qd2. However, it usually arises from a transposition from the Najdorf rather than the normal Scheveningen move order. Compared to the Keres, white has his bishop already developed to the e3 square while black has a pawn on a6 rather than a7.
The differences are subtle but critical. Now, the standard line of the Perenyi attack follows with 7...e5. This puts two attackers on the advanced g4 pawn (which only has the queen defending) and threatens the d4 knight. If this were the Keres, white could play the intermediate sequence 7. Bb5+ Bd7 8. Bxd7+ Qxd7, eliminating black's light squared bishop, a potential defender of the weak d5 square, and removing the guard from the f6 knight. White then continues with 9. Nf5, getting the knight out of danger and cutting off the queen's attack on the g4 pawn. Here, black would love to play 9...g6, chasing away the knight and then grabbing the g4 pawn, but it doesn't work. White could respond with either 10. Bg5, counterattacking the now undefending f6 knight, or 10. Ne3, defending the g4 pawn, and increasing white's hold on d5.
However, 8. Bb5+ is not an option here because of the a6 pawn. Therefore, white usually plays 8. Nf5, with the same idea of saving both the the knight and the g4 pawn. …

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/6B1/3NP3/2N2Q2/PP.text: The Dutch Variation is an aggressive variation of the Najdorf Sicilian where white aims to take black's knight doubling black's pawns on f7, when black tries to defend with moves like Nbd7 and Be7, white will play Be2, O-O-O, and g4, also, the move Rg1 is possible, because after Bxf6, white will play g5, and gain a tempo, if a piece takes, now, if after Bxf6, black play gxf6, then white will just keep in mind that black's doubled pawns are big weakness, and if in this variation, black decides to play the move O-O, then white can start a big attack, the only problem of this variation, is that if black plays carefully, they can achieve a drawish, or even a better position, depending on white's play.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/6B1/3NPP2/2N5/PPP.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4
Again, Black has to make a strategic choice. Common moves are :

7...Be7
7...Qc7
7...Nbd7
Two very sharp variations are seen at higher levels : 7...Qb6 (the Poisoned Pawn Variation) and 7...b5 (the Polugaevsky Variation).

r3kb1r/pp1qpppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QPB4/P.text:
Allowing the option of queenside castling, as well as Rc8 after castling kingside.
Nd2 is almost always played, although in a 1939 game, Aitken vs Flohr, white tried h3, and lost.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3n4/3P2b1/2N2N2/PP3P.text: White should play aggressively here, with 8. Qb3 being the key test. A passive move like 8. Be2 allows black to consolidate with a move such as 8... e6, and with the bishop outside the pawn chain, this is a pleasant isolated queen's pawn position for black.

r2qkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p3bp/8/3P3P/5NN1/PPP2P.text: 8. h5 is mostly played, aiming to tie up black's kingside pawns. The pawn on h5 is double-edged. It's powerfully positioned in black's territory, but it also requires protection from the knight on g3, making this potentially a bad piece.

rn1qkbnr/pp3pp1/2p1p1bp/8/3P3P/5NN1/PPP2.text: 7... e6 is less common as it lets the white knight onto e5, and 8. Ne5 is indeed the most common response. The familiar Caro-Kann themes of attacking black's light-square bishop, with either 8. h5 or 8. Bd3, are also commonly-played,

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1np1n2/1N2p1B1/4P3/2N5/.text: The primary purpose of 7...a6 is to drive the knight on b5 away from its strong position. The knight on b5 threatens to jump to c7, which would be a fork on Black's king and rook, and puts pressure on d6. By pushing the a-pawn, Black gains space on the queenside, which can support further pawn advances like ...b5, potentially leading to active counterplay on that side of the board. Forcing the knight to retreat diminishes White's immediate threats and allows Black to better organize their pieces. The knight typically moves to a3, where it is less active compared to b5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/2BNP3/2N1B3/P.text:
Black castles. White would like to continue their plan to long castle and assault Black's king side, but again they must take additional time to prepare it. Otherwise...
8. Qd2? to make way for long castling is answered with 8...Ng4!. This uncovers an attack on the knight on d4 while also attacking White's dark square bishop, which is a valuable piece needed to contest Black's bishop's control of the dark squares. To save the bishop, White is compelled to initiate the trade of knights themselves, 9. Nxc6 dxc6 10. Qxd8 (10. O-O-O?! Qxd2 11. Rxd2 Nxe3 loses the bishop pair anyway; 11. Bxd2?? hangs 11...Nxf2 with a fork) 10...Rxd8 11. Bg5 ⩲ and Black stands better.
White may try 8. f3?! to prevent ...Ng4, so that they can then play Qd2 and O-O-O. However, 8. f3 is answered with 8...Qb6!. This move attacks b2, so if e.g. 9. O-O? Qxb2! 10. Ncb5 Qb4 11. Be2 Nxd4 12. Nxd4 ± and Black escapes with a clean pawn. However the greater danger of 8...Qb6! is that it brings a second attacker to d4, and Black is ready to uncork a third. If 9. Qd2?? Nxe4! attacks the queen, while discovering an attack on d4 (10. fxe4 Bxd4 11. Bxd4 Qxd4 12. Qxd4 Nxd4 ±). 9. Bb5? is imaginative, but again falls afoul of 9...Nxe4! (10. fxe4 Bxd4 11. Bxd4 Qxd4 12. Qxd4 Nxd4 ±). The best try is 9. Bb3: 9...Nxe4 still follows, but White can at least recover the material with 10. Nd5 Qa5+ 11. c3 Nf6 12. Nxc6 dxc6 13. Nxe7+ ⩱.
Therefore White must begin with 8. Bb3. …

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/8/2PNP1n1/2N1B3/P.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 Ng4
This opening is ECO code B39.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1nppn2/1N6/2P1P3/2N5/PP.text:
7...a6 kicks White's knight.
Its available squares are d4 or a3.
The most common move is 8. Na3. This places a knight on the rim, but at least it overdefends c4 in case Black hopes to make use of the half-open file and play ...Rc8 one day.
8. Nd4 reduces White's control of d5, and allows Black to untangle with 8...d5 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nxd5 11. Nxc6 bxc6= (see diagram). The position is equal but now open, and White is no longer able to keep Black suffocating in their side of the board as they had hoped.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PP.text: The Belezky Line is a Yugoslav Attack sideline where black plays Nc6 instead of castling. White may continue with 8. Bc4, also trying to develop all their pieces before castling. This may be used as a weapon to make white question if black is going to castle at all.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PP.text:
The Yugoslav Attack continues with 7...O-O. In the Yugoslav, Black castles kingside while White castles queenside, leading to an opposite-side-castling game where speed is important. Black often pushes on the queenside with a5 and b5 and continues advancing those pawns, while White plays g4 and h4 and continues advancing those pawns. The fianchettoed bishop on g7 is a key piece in Black's attack on the queenside and what makes the Dragon the Dragon.
White's most popular continuation is 8. Qd2, preparing for a queenside castle.
Second is 8. Bc4, which often transposes to the main line.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p2pbn2/4p3/4P3/1NN1B3/PP.text:
Moves: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 Be6
This is the best move. The Black bishop covers d5 from e6 and also points at the queenside when White castles there. Black also contemplates using c4 as a piece outpost. Black's position retains maximum flexibility, as in almost all variations Black plays ...Be7, ...Nbd7, ...O-O, ...Rc8, and ...Nb6 in some order.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p2ppn2/1p4B1/3NPP2/2N5/PPP.text:
Moves : 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Bg5 e6 7. f4 b5
White has several possible choices. Common moves are :
8. e5 (main line)
8. Qf3
8. a3

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/pq1ppn2/6B1/3NPP2/2N5/PP.text:
Moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Qb6
Black launches a direct attack on the b2 pawn. White should defend it with 8. Nb3 or leave it to the enemy with 8. Qd2. This variation gained notoriety in the 1960s with Fischer's espousal of the system. His idea was that after grabbing a pawn, he could use his almost flawless technique to neutralize White's dangerous lead in development, and then win with his extra pawn and bishop pair.

rnbqk2r/1p2bppp/p2ppn2/6B1/3NPP2/2N5/PPP.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Be7
This used to be the main line, mostly out of Fischer's theoretical work. Today it is considered the sharpest line, with sacrifices on d5, b2, g7, and f7, and other such things. Mostly it is because of the large mass of variations that stem from this position. Today, however, the variation has rather fallen out of favor due to the increasing popularity of the Poisoned Pawn Variation after 7...Qb6.

r2qkb1r/pp1nnppp/2p1p1b1/3pP3/3P3N/8/PPP.text: Looking to move the knight to f3, as well as allowing c3, in support of the pawn at d4.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3n4/3P2b1/1QN2N2/PP3.text: White is creating threats, but black can create long-term weaknesses with 8... Bxf3. However, they will come under sustained pressure from white's attack.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1nppn2/8/2P1P3/N1N5/PP3.text:
White saves their knight with 8. Na3.
The position is looking cramped for Black. Those pawns on c4 and e4 prevent them from playing d5 and gaining more space. Meanwhile, Black's pawns on d6 and e6 prevent Black from developing their bishops very actively.
They have three typical continuations.
Black still has their bishops to develop, so option one is to develop their light-square bishop, in which case first Black must play 8...b6 to make room to fianchetto it.
Option two is to develop their dark-square bishop. Fianchettoing it is inconceivable of course because of how weak f6 will become. Since White induced them to play 5...d6, there is only one place left for it, so Black may as well play 8...Be7 and get it over with, then at least they can castle.
Option three is to discard both these options as too timid, throw caution at the wind, and kick open the Maroczy bind with 8...d5 anyway. This is an especially good continuation if it is 1985 and you are Garry Kasparov, after whom the audacious play, the Garry gambit, is named.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/PP.text:
Qd2 is the most popular continuation. White prepares to castle queenside, but typically doesn't play Bh6 to exchange bishops. This opposite-castling game leads to sharp attacking positions where the two side pawns open the king's castle.
Overwhelmingly popular (160 times more popular in the chess.com database than the second most popular) is 8...Nc6.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p2pbn2/4p3/4P3/1NN1BP2/P.text:
f3 might look like a slight inaccuracy. After all, never move the f-pawn right? As it turns out, this is by far the best move for white. f3 achieves multiple things at once:

Ng4, attempting to chop off the bishop, is now impossible.
e4 is now supported by a pawn instead of a piece (That might come under pressure in the future!)
If both sides castle on opposite sides, g4 and h4 are much easier to pull off.
In addition, the slight weakness created along the diagonal cannot be exploited by Black. The queen will take a lot of time to mobilize, and after Qh4+ g3 ends the attack right in its tracks. Like most of the English Attack, this move is directly taken from the Yugoslav Attack.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p2ppn2/1p2P1B1/3N1P2/2N5/P.text:
Moves : 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 b5 8.e5
A logical move which wants to attack the Black knight. Indeed this knight seems to be immobilized by the White bishop.
8...dxe5 (main line)

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/pq1ppn2/6B1/3NPP2/2N5/PP.text:
Moves:1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Qb6 8.Qd2
White allows Black to take the pawn. Having played 7...Qb6, Black should take the pawn now with 8...Qxb2. If Black radically changes plans and does not take the pawn, White will simply castle queenside (9. 0-0-0), protecting the pawn, and the Black queen will be out of place on b6, it would prefer to be on c7 where it doesn't obstruct the b-pawn.

r3kb1r/pp1q1ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QPB4/.text: With the light bishop now trapped,(this is also a drawback of the French Defense) black would like to exchange the bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3n4/3P4/1QN2b2/PP3PP.text: White is committed to the attack, and must accept the doubled, isolated pawns. Beware the tempting 9. Qxb7, which loses on the spot to 9... Ndb4, and white's queen is trapped.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppb/2p4p/7P/3P4/5NN1/PPP2PP.text: 9. Bd3 is almost always played. Black has spent numerous tempos on this bishop, and since white usually aims to castle queenside, it makes sense to remove the light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1pn2/3p4/2P1P3/N1N5/P.text:
Black challenges White in the centre to open up the position.
White has four attackers to Black's three defenders. However, after 9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5, Black intends to play 10...Nb4, bringing another attacker.

**History**
The Garry gambit was first played by Garry Kasparov in two games of the 1985 World Championship match with Anatoly Karpov (see sample game).
After the discovery of the continuation 12. Be3 Bxe3 13. Qa4+! (see below) this fell out of favour for Black.


**Karpov v Kasparov, 1985**
The sixteenth game of the World Championship match.
1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nc6 5. Nb5 d6 6. c4 Nf6 7. N1c3 a6 8. Na3 d5
Kasparov plays the "Garry gambit".

9. cxd5 exd5 10. exd5 Nb4
This position had already been reached in their twelfth game of the match. In that game, Karpov (playing White) continued 11. Bc4, a natural move to defend the pawn, and continued cautiously before having to settle for a draw: 11...Bg4 (compelling White's bishop to retreat) 12. Be2 Bxe2 13. Qxe2+ Qe7 14. Be3 Nbxd5 (Black recovers the pawn) 15. Nc2 Nxe3 16. Nxe3 Qe6 17. O-O Bc5 18. Rfe1 O-O ½-½.
11. Be2
This time White intends to control d5 with a Be2-Bf3 manoeuvre.
11...Bc5
Rather than take back the pawn, Black leaves it and focuses on development instead. They can quickly capitalise on good, active squares for their pieces, while White's knight on a3 is passive.
Kasparov analysed 11...Nbxd5 12. O-O Be7 13. Nxd5 Nxd5 14. Bf3 (attacking knight) Be6 (defending knight) 15. …

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/8/3NP3/2N1BP2/P.text:
Both sides have now sufficiently developed and white faces a major dilemma for their next move:
- 9. Bc4 was originally the most popular and critical line. White controls d5 as much as possible, trying to restrict all central counterplay from white. The mainline then follows 9...Bd7 10. 0-0-0 Rc8 11. Bb3 and both sides go on an all out attack on each other's king.
- 9. 0-0-0 was seen until recently a refuted line that allowed black to immediately equalize and avoid the massive pawn storm coming at them. With the advent of engines it was revealed that white actually maintains a larger, positional advantage. This led to a theory war with many top players trying to find deep ideas for each color up until the endgame.
- 9. g4 is a hyper aggressive variation that has the very simple and easy idea of punching black in the face as soon as possible by immediately going on the offensive. This variation is known for being extremely dangerous to both sides, but engine analysis has shown that black has sufficient counterplay in the center to survive the attack easily.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p3pn2/1p2p1B1/3N1P2/2N5/PP.text:
Moves : 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Bg5 e6 7. f4 b5 8. e5 dxe5
Now the following move is very logical in the main line of Polougaevsky Variation :
9. fxe5 (main line)

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/6B1/3NPP2/2N5/PqP.text:
The famous Poisoned Pawn Variation. Black accepts the pawn. This line after good results from Black, initially Fischer but later Kasparov has seen a decline in popularity of 6.Bg5.
The line was popularized by Bobby Fischer, who in playing this line said that he could grab a pawn, give his opponent three or four moves in development, and still win! Today the line is just as messy as it was in its heyday in the 1970s, but is now considered to be equal with best play. Today there have been lines analyzed up to twenty or thirty moves in depth, such as this one, the main one.

r3kb1r/pp1q1ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P1Bb1/1QPB1N.text: With the light bishop now trapped, black would like to exchange the bishop, so Bxf3 is most common, although this can be delayed.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3n4/3P4/1QN2P2/PP3P1.text: White now has a poor pawn structure, but also has numerous threats. Best here is to allow white to take the b7 pawn by defending the knight with 9... e6. 9... Nb6 is also an option, but 10. d5 creates many challenges for Black. Note that 9... Nxc3 is a mistake allowing both 10. bxc3 or even 10. Qxb7 with advantage for white.

r2qkbnr/pp1npppb/2p4p/7P/3P4/3B1NN1/PPP2.text: Black's almost invariable response of 9...Bxd3 is almost forced, although 9...Ngf6 and even 9...e6 have both been attempted, without much success.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/8/2BNP3/2N1BP2/.text: Bc4 develops the bishop to a good square, pinning the f7 pawn and aiming at the Black king and kingside to attack. On the next move White will castle queenside and a fierce attack is on!

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p3pn2/1p2P1B1/3N4/2N5/PPP3.text:
Moves : 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 b5 8.e5 dxe5 9. fxe5
Now Black has a very tactical move (main line):
9...Qc7 (main line)

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/6B1/3NPP2/2N5/PqP.text: The most popular move. After 9.Rb1 White chases away the Black queen and assumes control of the b-file. After the queen escapes to a3 (only move), White will have several options.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3n4/3P4/1QN2P2/PP3P.text: White has a poor pawn structure but strong pressure, and needs to force the issue. 10. Qxb7 is almost always played here.

r2qkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p4p/7P/3P4/3b1NN1/PPP2.text: Taking with the queen is of course the only response, to prevent the doubled, isolated pawns.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/2BNP3/2N1BP2/.text: Bd7 develops the bishop to its only good square at the moment. This  move also has a second purpose: to free the c8 square for the rook. In the Open Sicilians, Black gets a half open c-file in exchange for White's half-open d-file, and Bd7/Rc8 is a good way to take advantage of it. Rc8 also threatens White's c4-bishop, forcing it to move out of danger with most commonly Bb3.

rnb1kb1r/2q2ppp/p3pn2/1p2P1B1/3N4/2N5/PP.text:
Moves : 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Bg5 e6 7. f4 b5 8. e5 dxe5 9. fxe5 Qc7.
Now White seems to gain space and Black seems to be undeveloped. But the following moves will show that its not so evident.
10. exf6 (main line)

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/p2ppn2/6B1/3NPP2/q1N5/P1.text:
This is the only move for Black's queen, and so should be self explanatory. Another move, 9...Nxe4? drops a piece not to 10.Nxe4?? Qxb1+ and Black is winning, but 10.Rxb2 Nxd2 11.Kxd2 and White is winning.
Here White has a few choices. The most popular is 10.f5, applying direct pressure to e6. Then Black usually plays 10...Nc6 11.fxe6 fxe6 12.Nxc6 bxc6 13.e5 dxe5 14.Bxf6 gxf6 15.Ne4, when Black's best is 15...Qxa2 (or 15...Be7 16.Be2 h5 17.Rf1!, with a strong attack).
White's other choices are 10.e5 and 10.Bxf6.

r2qkbnr/pp1nppp1/2p4p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PPP2.text: Previously, all three main responses (...Ngf6, ...e6, ...Qc7) were thought to be equivalent, and often transposed to the same position with black castling queenside. Later development saw Black look at castling kingside, but for a while this fell out of favour as White found he could move his knight to e4 or e2, and advance g4, without needing to prepare Rg1. This extra tempo seems to threaten this line as a viable alternative for black, as white can win the race between the white kingside and black queenside attacks. More recent theory, however, has seen Black resurrect ...e6, quite often not castling at all, while the other alternatives remain out of favour.

r2q1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/2BNP3/2N1BP2/.text: White castles queenside. Black should aim at White's king with Rc8 or Qa5 next, but other moves such as Ne5 are possible. Both sides often use their pawns on a6 and b6 (Black) or g2 and h2 (White) to open lines on the side they are attacking.

rnb1kb1r/2q2ppp/p3pP2/1p4B1/3N4/2N5/PPP3.text:
Moves : 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 b5 8.e5 dxe5 9. fxe5 Qc7 10. exf6
Now Black has a logical move which explains the move 9...Qc7:
10...Qe5+
Indeed, after this move Black will capture a figure : Bishop (in the main line) or a Knight.
So, the material will be recovered.

r3k2r/pp3ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/3P2b1/1QPB1N2/PP.text: White can either castle, the usual response, or prepare the queen for some shuffling around by accepting the gambit.

r2qkbnr/pp1n1pp1/2p1p2p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PP.text: 11. Bf4 is the most challenging response  when faced with modern Black theory where Black does not castle queenside. In earlier theory, when Black planned to castle queenside, Bd2 was almost equivalent. The other alternatives offer little for White.

r3kbnr/ppqnppp1/2p4p/7P/3P4/3Q1NN1/PPP2P.text:
With this move, black develops a piece, prepares possible queenside castling, and prevents the white bishop from coming to f4, which could be problematic for black's king should he castle long. White's two main options from here include:

11. Bd2 - The standard, main line move.
11. Rh4!? - A less common, aggressive move sometimes seen in professional play. White intends to swing the rook out to help pressure a black target.

2rq1rk1/pp1bppbp/2np1np1/8/2BNP3/2N1BP2/.text: Black takes advantage of the half-open c-file they received in the Open Sicilian, and aims at the hanging c4-bishop. As Nxd4 Qxd4 Ng4! takes advantage of the overworked White queen and Black is attacking both bishops at once, White typically moves the bishop to safety with Bb3, keeping an eye on the Black king.

rnb1kb1r/5ppp/p3pP2/1p2q1B1/3N4/2N5/PPP3.text:
Moves : 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6 5. Nc3 a6 6. Bg5 e6 7. f4 b5 8. e5 dxe5 9. fxe5 Qc7 10. exf6 Qe5+
White has to protect the King so a figure will be lost :
11. Be2 (main line)

r3k2r/pQ3ppp/2nqpn2/3p4/3P2b1/2PB1N2/PP1.text:
White accepted the gambit in Ilja Schneider (2368) vs Peter Kuehn (2384), played in the European Club Cup, in 2006. The game continued:
